subChunks.title: Entity-Relationship Diagrams & Schema Design
subChunks.hookHtml: Before you write a single CREATE TABLE statement, you need to know what you are modelling. Entity-relationship design is the discipline of turning real-world concepts into a structured schema before touching the database.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Entities, Attributes & Relationships

An entity is a thing you need to track (Mage, Spell, Enrolment). An attribute is a property of an entity (name, damage, enrolledAt). A relationship connects entities (a Mage casts many Spells).

Relationship Types

  • One-to-One (1:1): Each Mage has exactly one Profile. Each Profile belongs to exactly one Mage.
  • One-to-Many (1:N): One Topic has many Chunks. Each Chunk belongs to one Topic.
  • Many-to-Many (M:N): A Mage can learn many Spells; a Spell can be learned by many Mages. Requires a junction table (mage_spells).

Choosing Primary Keys

Use a surrogate key (generated UUID or auto-increment integer) rather than a natural key (name, email) unless the natural key is guaranteed to be unique and immutable. Names change. Emails change. A UUID never changes after creation.

Schema Design Process

  1. List all entities the system needs to track
  2. For each entity, list its attributes and identify the primary key
  3. Identify relationships between entities and their cardinality (1:1, 1:N, M:N)
  4. For M:N relationships, create a junction table
  5. Decide on foreign key constraints and whether to cascade deletes

Indexing

Indexes speed up reads but slow down writes. Add an index on columns you will WHERE, JOIN, or ORDER BY frequently. Always index foreign key columns.

CREATE INDEX idx_spells_tier ON spells(tier);
CREATE INDEX idx_assignments_mage ON spell_assignments(mage_id);

storyBeats.text: Before the Academy's new records system was built, its architect spent two weeks at a drawing board. No code was written. Only diagrams.

storyBeats.speaker: Systems Architect Mela
storyBeats.text: Data modelling comes before schema design. What are the entities? What are their attributes? How do they relate? A one-to-many? A many-to-many? Draw this out. A poorly modelled schema cannot be fixed by clever SQL — you will be fighting it for the life of the system.

storyBeats.speaker: Academy data model sketch
Systems Architect Mela
storyBeats.text: Surrogate keys — UUIDs or auto-increment integers — are almost always preferable to natural keys. A mage's name might be unique today, but the Academy may decide to allow duplicates tomorrow. A UUID never needs to change, so foreign keys referencing it are safe forever.

learningObjectives: Identify entities and attributes from a natural language problem description
Classify relationships as 1:1, 1:N, or M:N and design the correct schema for each
Create a junction table for a many-to-many relationship
Choose between surrogate and natural primary keys and justify the choice
Know when to add a database index and what trade-off it represents
commonMistakes: Using natural keys (name, email) that might change — invalidates all foreign key references when they change
Storing M:N relationships in a comma-separated column — violates normalisation and makes JOINs impossible
Adding indexes on every column 'for performance' — indexes cost write performance and storage
Forgetting the junction table for M:N relationships and trying to model it in one of the two tables
assessmentCriteria: Can read a natural language description of a domain and produce a correct ER diagram (entities, attributes, relationships, cardinalities)
Can write CREATE TABLE statements for a 1:N and M:N relationship including foreign key constraints
Can explain why a junction table is needed for M:N and what columns it contains
Can articulate the trade-off between read performance (indexes) and write performance
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain entity-relationship modelling to a junior developer who has only ever worked with single tables. What are the three relationship types? Why does a many-to-many relationship require a junction table? Give a concrete real-world example.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Design a schema for the following domain: An online bookshop sells books. Each book has a title, ISBN, and price. Books belong to one or more genres. Authors write books (a book can have multiple authors). Customers can place orders; each order contains one or more books with a quantity.

Write out:

  1. A list of entities and their key attributes
  2. The relationship type between each pair of entities
  3. CREATE TABLE statements for all tables (use INTEGER primary keys; note which columns need foreign keys)
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Design a schema for a Hospital Appointment System: Patients have a name, date of birth, and NHS number. Doctors have a name, specialisation, and GMC number. Appointments link a patient to a doctor at a specific date/time, with a status (SCHEDULED, COMPLETED, CANCELLED). A patient can see many doctors over time; a doctor sees many patients.

Write: entity list with attributes, relationship types, and full CREATE TABLE statements with appropriate foreign keys. Include at least one index you would add and explain why.

questions.questionHtml: A Student can enrol in many Courses, and a Course can have many Students. What relationship type is this?
questions.explanationHtml: When both sides of a relationship can have multiple instances of the other, it is Many-to-Many (M:N). This requires a junction (association) table — in this case enrolments(student_id, course_id).

questions.questionHtml: Why is using a user's email address as a primary key usually a bad idea?
options: Email addresses are too long for database storage
Email addresses can change, and all foreign key references would need updating
SQL does not support VARCHAR primary keys
Email addresses are not unique enough
questions.correctAnswer: Email addresses can change, and all foreign key references would need updating
questions.explanationHtml: Natural keys like email or username are risky primary keys because they can change. When a natural key changes, every foreign key referencing it must also be updated — a cascading problem. Surrogate keys (UUID or auto-increment) never change and make updates to user details trivially safe.

questions.questionHtml: You notice that updating a customer's city in the orders table requires changing 50 rows. What does this indicate?
options: The database is performing correctly — orders should store city
The table is denormalised — city belongs in a customers table referenced by a foreign key
You need a trigger to update all rows automatically
The city column should be removed entirely
questions.correctAnswer: The table is denormalised — city belongs in a customers table referenced by a foreign key
questions.explanationHtml: Needing to update many rows to change one logical fact is a clear sign of denormalisation. City should live in one place (the customers table). All order rows reference the customer by ID; the city is fetched via a JOIN at query time.
